questions: How does the Greyquill Method work?
How do you actually run an engagement?
answers.answer: Three sequenced phases, each run by one layer of the platform. Foundation gives every model a record it can stand on, using GQData. Govern turns your rules into controls the system can prove it followed, using GQ Govern. Activate ships the use case with oversight that scales, using GQ Agents. Each phase targets a specific place AI projects die.

questions: Why do most AI projects fail?
Why do only 5 in 100 GenAI ideas reach production?
What goes wrong with enterprise AI?
answers.answer: Of every 100 GenAI ideas started, roughly 5 reach production. About 40 are lost because the data was never AI-ready, 35 fall over at evaluation when nobody can evidence that controls held, and 20 die in production without oversight. The Method maps one phase onto each of those three failures.

questions: Tell me about your data product
How do you make data AI-ready?
answers.answer: GQData is the trusted-data layer beneath every AI decision. It unifies master data into golden records, repairs quality at source rather than downstream, stamps active lineage on what your models consume, and classifies sensitivity. It is the Foundation tier that GQ Govern and GQ Agents both build on.

questions: How do you handle AI governance?
answers.answer: GQ Govern turns a written policy into something the system can produce evidence for. Controls are checked against frameworks including the EU AI Act, GDPR, and SOC 2, and each control is tied to the policy that enforces it. Exceptions carry an expiry rather than becoming a permanent bypass.

questions: How do you run agents safely in production?
answers.answer: GQ Agents is the Activate tier: productionised generative and agentic workloads with oversight that scales. Evidence is assembled while the agent runs rather than reconstructed afterwards, so provenance, checkpoints, and an audit trail exist by the time anyone asks for them.

questions: Do you work in regulated industries?
Do you work in banking or financial services?
Have you shipped in telecom or retail?
answers.answer: Yes, that is the whole focus. We have shipped governed AI in production across BFSI, telecom, and retail, and have delivered in healthcare and public sector work where the governance bar is just as high. The platform exists because regulated enterprises need AI they can put in front of an auditor.

questions: Does my data leave my environment?
Do we have to move our data to you?
What about data residency and sovereignty?
answers.answer: Your data stays where it is. The platform installs into your own environment, meaning your cloud account, your region, and your identity provider, and reads data in place. There is no requirement to ship raw copies to us.

questions: How do I book a call?
What does your discovery process look like?
answers.answer: Start with a 30-minute discovery call. Bring your hardest data or policy question and we will tell you honestly whether the bottleneck is data, process, or model. Fuller discovery adds stakeholder interviews, a working session with the team that owns the problem, and a business and technical analysis. We do not write code until everyone agrees on what we are building.

questions: I need to be Greyquill certified
Is there a Greyquill certification programme?
Do you run training for our team?
answers.answer: We do not run a Greyquill certification programme. We do run training as part of consulting engagements, including workshops and enablement so your team can operate what we build once we hand it over. If you have something specific in mind, a short call is the fastest way to scope it.

questions: How do I become a partner?
Do you have a partner programme?
I want to work with Greyquill
answers.answer: We work with technology and delivery partners, and the partnerships page sets out who we already build alongside. There is no self-serve partner programme to sign up to, so the route is a direct conversation about what you have in mind.

questions: How do I get in touch?
How do I reach the team?
answers.answer: Email us at hello@greyquill.io or send a note through the contact page, and if you would rather talk it through, a 30-minute discovery call is easy to book.

questions: Do you have a phone number?
I need to speak to someone
Is there a number I can call?
This is urgent, how do I reach you quickly?
answers.answer: You can call us on +91 80505 22809, though email at hello@greyquill.io or a booked 30-minute discovery call usually gets you a fuller answer.

questions: What other products do you have?
Show me your full product range
What is in the Greyquill platform?
answers.answer: Four platform layers, and four things built on them. GQData is the trusted-data layer beneath every AI decision. GQ Govern is the policy layer that makes AI defensible. GQ Agents handles multi-agent orchestration with audit trails built in. GQ Studio is one application shell for the whole platform. Three vertical products sit on top: GST Co-Pilot for GST reconciliation, Commerce Synapse for retail and commerce operations, and Umami for clinical practice management. ClarityAI stands alone, scoring the clarity and risk of an initiative before you fund it.

questions: How do the three products fit together?
answers.answer: GQ Studio is the single application shell over the whole platform: the workspaces, screens, and low-code customization layer that tie GQData, GQ Govern, and GQ Agents into one product experience. It is where data engineers, stewards, compliance officers, and AI engineers all work on the same records against the same trail. It ships with the platform rather than being sold on its own.

questions: Tell me about your GST product
Do you have anything for Indian tax?
What does the GST co-pilot actually do?
answers.answer: GST Co-Pilot is a four-agent system for Indian GST work: invoice ingestion, extraction, GSTR-2B reconciliation, and exception resolution. An orchestrator reads intent, routes work, and escalates to a human reviewer above a configurable threshold. It compresses the forty-plus hours a month an average mid-market tax team spends on manual reconciliation into an afternoon, and it is our reference architecture for governed agentic AI in production.

questions: How do you match invoices to GSTR-2B?
What if the invoice number is formatted differently?
answers.answer: Five passes, each less strict than the last, and each one works only on what earlier passes left behind. Pass one matches the e-invoice IRN at full confidence. Pass two matches GSTIN plus a normalised invoice number and value within a rupee. Pass three allows a fuzzy invoice number. Pass four uses amount and date. Pass five is amount only and always goes to a reviewer.

questions: What happens when an invoice is missing from GSTR-2B?
How do you handle ITC risk?
What if my vendor has not filed?
answers.answer: Your purchase register is compared against the GSTR-2B the portal publishes from vendor filings. Anything still unmatched is checked against adjacent periods first, since late filing is common, then classified as missing in GSTR-2B or missing in books. Each one is scored zero to a hundred for ITC risk and given a priority and an SLA, so critical items reach the finance team first.

questions: Tell me about the Champ agent swarm
Do you use AI to build software?
How does the agent swarm work?
answers.answer: Champ is our peer-based agent swarm for end-to-end software delivery. Agents talk through work packets on a shared board, with no hierarchy. Champ decomposes a PRD into packets, dispatches them, and watches progress. Specialist agents cover architecture, development, QA, PR review, and deployment, several running their own mini-swarms. Every packet carries a unique id, a phase history, and an append-only event log entry.

questions: How do you test your agents?
How do you know an agent actually did the work?
How are agents verified before deployment?
Do you keep auditing agents after launch?
answers.answer: An agent reporting done has told you about its confidence. So every result passes through a harness the agent does not control: it works in a sealed sandbox with a written brief and a time budget, then a separate grader inspects the artefacts it left and returns pass or fail. Before a check ships, a do-nothing agent has to fail it and a correct answer has to pass it.

questions: Do you have a retail product?
answers.answer: Commerce Synapse is our retail and commerce vertical product: AI-orchestrated commerce operations on a trusted product and customer foundation, so operations, pricing, and merchandising decisions all run on unified data. Like GST Co-Pilot, it is a reference architecture for governed agentic AI in a real domain, built on the Greyquill platform. It lives at its own address, linked from the products page.

questions: Tell me about your health platform
answers.answer: Umami is our healthcare vertical product: AI-powered practice management for medical clinics, with audit trails and clinical-workflow controls built in. The Document Center publishes its data model, which maps real-world concepts like doctor, nurse, and hospital onto a FHIR-aligned entity model organised by domain. We have shipped in healthcare, though we do not claim deep references in that vertical yet.

questions: How do I score an AI initiative?
answers.answer: ClarityAI scores the clarity and risk of an initiative before you fund it. Drop in a PRD, AI brief, RFP, or statement of work as PDF, DOCX, or plain text and it returns a clarity score, line-by-line fixes, and a one-page go, hold, or kill summary. It scores ambiguity, testability, edge-case coverage, regulatory exposure, and dependency risk. It works standalone, with no signup.

questions: What does your digital transformation service cover?
Can you modernise our old systems?
How do you handle a legacy rewrite?
answers.answer: We modernise the systems you already run, step by step. Map the estate, pick one seam with a small blast radius, build alongside it behind a clean interface, run old and new against the same work until the numbers reconcile, then retire the legacy piece and repeat. That covers legacy application modernisation, process automation, systems and data integration, and cloud migration. No big-bang rewrites.

questions: What does your AI and data service cover?
Do you run AI training or workshops?
Where should we start with AI?
answers.answer: Twelve engagements across training, assessments, and consulting, organised in five phases from boardroom to production: Align, Diagnose, Plan, Build, Ship. Most clients start at Phase 01 and can stop at any milestone. The later phases are build phases run by the same engineers who build the platform, covering LLM applications and retrieval, agentic systems, master data and lineage, and evaluation and monitoring.

questions: What does your product engineering service cover?
Can you add AI features to our existing product?
answers.answer: Discovery to design to production, with one senior team owning the outcome. Discovery and scoping workshops, UX and product design, web, mobile, and backend engineering, AI-native features that ship with evaluation, guardrails, and an audit trail, QA and reliability, then DevOps. Every brief runs through ClarityAI first. After launch we can stay on as the product team, and everything is yours to own.

questions: What have you done in BFSI?
answers.answer: Banking, financial services, and payments, where AI lives or dies on auditability. We have built a multi-rail payment processing layer handling tens of thousands of transactions per minute, and a reconciliation engine with rule-based first-pass matching, ML-assisted fuzzy matching, and a human review queue carrying lineage on every decision. The regulatory ground includes RBI, SEBI, DPDP, FCA, PRA, FFIEC, OCC, PCI-DSS, and Basel III.

questions: What have you done in telecom?
Can you help modernise a telecom platform?
Do you do churn or agent assist?
answers.answer: Telecom estates carry decades of legacy and customer data spread across a dozen systems. We have retired pieces of an aging platform module by module while the business kept running, built a master-data layer unifying customer identity across CRM, billing, and OSS, and replaced brittle RPA scripts with multi-agent orchestrations that ask a human when uncertain. Identity gets reconciled before any model is allowed to act.

questions: What have you done for retailers?
Can you help with dashboard sprawl?
answers.answer: Retail decisions repeat daily across millions of SKUs and customers. We have mapped and simplified overlapping operational workflows at a retailer that grew by acquisition, consolidated dozens of conflicting dashboards into one decision surface on a governed data layer, and fused point-of-sale, e-commerce, and supplier signals with lineage under ML-assisted demand forecasting. Consolidation usually beats new analytics.

questions: How long does a project take?
How quickly can we see something?
How long until we go live?
answers.answer: It depends on scope and complexity. A typical custom build runs three to six months from discovery to deployment, and smaller assessments or training engagements run in weeks. On the platform we aim at one governed entity serving through the API as the first milestone, because that proves the whole chain end to end. You get a specific timeline at the end of discovery.

We do not publish rates. Quotes are scoped after discovery, with defined payment milestones, itemised invoices, and no hidden fees, and pricing is value-based against the business outcome. Use the contact form and pick Request a quote, with enough detail about the project for us to give a meaningful estimate. We are also upfront that we are not the cheapest option.

questions: Do you support what you build?
answers.answer: Yes. We walk alongside clients through the operating life of the software, and most of our work is repeat work. Options include maintenance agreements, enhancement work, and training so your team can run the system on their own. Every engagement carries defined SLAs for issue response and resolution, regular maintenance and security updates, multiple support channels, and a warranty period on what we deliver.

questions: Will your security team talk to ours?
answers.answer: Security and privacy are built into every engagement. We follow secure development practices, encrypt sensitive data, and align with the regulations relevant to your jurisdiction, including GDPR, DPDP, CCPA, and PCI-DSS. The platform installs into your own environment, so records, lineage, and the audit trail never cross our boundary, and authentication runs through your own identity provider over OAuth2 and OIDC.

We are a Silver-tier IBM Partner Plus member, and our engineers hold current certifications across the stack we ship on: watsonx.ai, watsonx.data, watsonx.data intelligence, watsonx.data integration, watsonx.governance, IBM Verify, and IBM Business Automation. On frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001, GQ Govern checks controls against them for you. Bring your own audit requirements and we will answer them directly.

questions: Which compliance frameworks do you support?
Do you cover the EU AI Act?
What standards can you check against?
answers.answer: Five standards are checkable today in GQ Govern: the EU AI Act, GDPR, SOC 2, ISO 27001, and India's DPDP Act, with dozens more mapped by domain and region so a workspace can find the one it actually needs. Each pass names the policy enforcing it, and a miss becomes a documented exception with a reason, a compensating action, a target date, and a named approver.

questions: Can you work with our existing systems?
Will this integrate with our legacy core?
Does this replace our data warehouse?
Do we have to rip anything out?
answers.answer: Yes. Most of what we build layers onto existing estates: legacy core systems, OSS/BSS, ERPs, data warehouses, and identity providers. Where a legacy system cannot change, we put an API facade in front of it and move data over event-driven pipelines. GQ Studio sits alongside your warehouse or lake, reading from your systems of record and serving governed entities out.

questions: Tell me about the IBM partnership
What does built on IBM foundations mean?
answers.answer: We are a Silver-tier IBM Partner Plus member, certified across watsonx and IBM Verify. We chose that foundation because watsonx carries lineage, model governance, and audit primitives risk and compliance teams already recognise, which is less work to defend. Your data, governance configuration, and agent definitions stay yours. We use the IBM stack where it earns its place and compose with other systems where they are stronger.

We are an enterprise AI consulting firm and an IBM Business Partner based in Bengaluru, working with regulated organisations across banking, insurance, retail, and telecom. Four founding engineers cover architecture, business analysis, infrastructure, and design, backed by a wider delivery team, with fifty-plus years of combined experience shipping enterprise software in regulated sectors. We are a consulting firm as much as a product team, and at this stage that matters.

We install into your environment: your cloud account, your region, your identity provider, your keys. The major clouds are supported and the pattern is the same on each, with on-prem and air-gapped topologies covered in the architecture brief. Containers run on Red Hat OpenShift with namespace-per-tenant isolation. Every source is residency-checked when it is connected, then enforced on every read after that.

questions: Do you have an architecture document?
Can I get something for my CISO?
What can I share with InfoSec?
answers.answer: Yes. The architecture and governance brief runs two to three pages, written for whoever inside your organisation approves this before procurement signs. It covers deployment topology across your cloud, on-prem, or air-gapped, data residency, the IBM stack components used and which are replaceable, identity and SSO with your own IdP, audit evidence flow, and what you take with you when the engagement ends.

questions: Where can I read more technical detail?
answers.answer: The Document Center is a curated space for open Greyquill material. It carries the GQ Studio product preview, platform and architecture documents including the C4 model and the GQ Data build explainer, five method documents on how we build, four on the Champ agent swarm, five on GST Co-Pilot's architecture and engine, and the FHIR-aligned healthcare data model. Every method page has a one-page PDF summary.

questions: How do you replace a legacy system safely?
How do you avoid a big-bang rewrite?
How do you prove the new system is right?
answers.answer: It is how we replace a legacy system without a big-bang rewrite. Pick a seam, build the replacement behind a facade, then have both process the same real work and classify every difference: a match, a tolerable difference, a defect in the replacement, or a defect in the legacy that has run for years. You cut over once real divergences hold at zero across a full business cycle.

questions: How do you map a legacy estate?
Where do you start with modernisation?
How do you find undocumented dependencies?
Do we need a discovery tool for that?
answers.answer: Before touching a legacy estate we write down what actually exists: six columns per system, covering every inbound and outbound path including manual uploads, email attachments, and someone rekeying from a screen. Interviews miss the systems nobody has thought about in years, so we also read firewall and DNS config, scheduled jobs, and database accounts. A filled-in spreadsheet beats a discovery platform nobody has populated.

questions: How do you decide what to automate?
When does a human stay in the loop?
How do you set a confidence threshold?
answers.answer: Map the process first, then sort each step: deterministic steps become plain software, judgement steps get agents, and some steps stay with a person. Judgement steps get a confidence line, and everything below it goes to review. Start with a shadow period where everything is reviewed, read the agreement rate by confidence band, set the line, then move it on evidence with a named approver and a date.

questions: What do we get out of discovery?
answers.answer: Five days of structured questioning that turn an idea into something a team can build from and a sponsor can fund. Day one fixes the outcome and how anyone would know it landed. Day two walks the workflow end to end with the people who perform it. Day three collects constraints, day four weighs at least two routes, day five sets scope, order, and estimate.

questions: When is an AI feature done?
What is your definition of done for AI?
How do you test AI features?
What gates does an AI feature pass?
answers.answer: A normal definition of done assumes a feature passing today will pass tomorrow, and a model breaks that. So we gate on an evaluation set written before the build finished, a grader proven to fail a wrong answer, repeated runs with the spread recorded, a test that attempts each guardrail, an exercised failure path, and a record of every decision. Cost and latency at peak are advisory gates.

questions: What happens if we stop working with you?
Can we take our data out?
What do we keep at the end?
answers.answer: You keep everything. Clients receive full ownership of custom-developed code on completion, and golden records, lineage, and the full audit trail export in open formats whenever you ask for them. Your governance configuration and agent definitions are yours as well. Open standards run across the stack, so the evidence belongs to you rather than being something you rent from us.

questions: Do you have anything for my industry?
How do you adapt to a new domain?
Can we bring our own data model?
answers.answer: The platform underneath is the same everywhere. What changes by industry is the pack: the entity model, the survivorship defaults, the control set, and the workflows you start from. A pack is configuration rather than a fork, so you keep getting platform improvements as they land, and a new industry means writing a new pack with no change to the engine. Insurance claims is the first one.

questions: Which languages do you work in?
answers.answer: Go, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript, with React, Next.js and Node.js on the web, and Flutter or React Native on mobile. PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, MongoDB and Redis for data. AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and IBM Cloud for hosting. Jenkins, CircleCI, GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Ansible for delivery. That is the shortlist rather than the limit, so ask about yours.

We are early, so there are no logos or testimonials yet. Customer names stay withheld, though the patterns are real: a multi-rail payments platform, a telecom modernisation carried out while the platform stayed in production, retail process and reporting consolidation. GQ Studio is in product preview with a small number of design partners. If you want a reference before signing, we may not have one and will say so.

entries.heading: Why we exist.
entries.text: Why we exist.. We have spent our careers building enterprise-grade software for banking, financial services, insurance, retail, and telecom. Most of those projects shipped. Most of those clients came back. Even on the wins, our team kept asking the same question. How could this have gone better? Where did vague requirements cost us a week? Where did a misalignment we should have caught earlier eat into the timeline? We are perfectionists, and the hardest critic of any Greyquill engagement has always been the Greyquill team that ran it. Alongside our own work, we watched other teams and other companies ship projects that did not land. The root cause was almost always the same: nobody truly understood what needed to be built. Vague requirements, misaligned stakeholders, assumptions instead of facts. Six months later, software that technically worked but did not solve the actual problem.

entries.heading: The lessons that survived contact with production.
entries.text: The lessons that survived contact with production.. Reconciliation is where governance gets tested. The hard cases hide in the small percentage of transactions that fail to match, and any AI assist has to explain itself line by line or risk teams will never sign off. Legacy core systems leak context at every integration boundary. Before any model can be trusted, the data crossing those boundaries needs lineage and a single, durable definition. "Faster approvals" is the wrong KPI for governed AI in BFSI. Audit completeness and time-to-evidence matter more, because that is what regulators actually ask for under examination. In payments, throughput and provenance are equally non-negotiable. Designs that win on one and lose on the other do not ship past production review. Solutions we have delivered

Demand and supply teams optimize against each other when the underlying data does not match. A shared data definition is the cheapest forecasting improvement available. Process re-engineering is where retail AI actually compounds. Models that bolt onto a broken process inherit the brokenness. Solutions we have delivered

entries.heading: The hard part comes after the model works
entries.text: The hard part comes after the model works. Most AI programmes get the model right. What stops them is the review. Someone in risk or internal audit asks where a figure came from, and answering means pulling exports from four systems and reconstructing the path by hand. That takes weeks, and the momentum behind the project usually does not survive it. The EU AI Act has turned that question into a legal one. It expects training data you can trace, human oversight on high-impact decisions, and technical documentation that matches how the system actually runs. Most data platforms were never designed to answer on demand, so the evidence gets assembled by hand every time somebody asks for it. We built GQ Studio around the evidence instead. entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Connecting the systems you already run
entries.text: Connecting the systems you already run. Everything starts here. You point the workspace at your systems of record, or create managed storage inside it when there is nothing to point at yet. Connectors cover the shape most enterprise estates actually have. Change data capture off a relational system of record, nightly batch out of object storage, REST from a SaaS CRM, and a direct path into finance. Every source is residency-checked before the first byte is read, and locked to the region the workspace runs in. Managed storage is provisioned in your own subscription inside that same region, encrypted with workspace-managed keys, versioned, and immutable once ingested. Records that fail your ingestion rules go to quarantine with the reason attached, so nothing broken enters the pipeline quietly and nothing gets dropped on the floor either. Connections, syncs and schema changes all land on the audit trail.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Resolution a steward can stand behind
entries.text: Resolution a steward can stand behind. Matching handles most of the volume on its own. What is left is judgement, so the product puts it in front of a person. Anything above your auto-merge threshold merges without asking. Everything below it waits in a queue with the match evidence attached, so the steward can see why the system thought these were the same entity in the first place. The steward chooses the surviving value field by field, with the source and the last-updated date sitting next to each candidate. Survivorship defaults come from the vertical pack, so most fields are already decided. A manual pick overrides the default and is attributed to whoever made it. That choice becomes part of the record's history and travels with it from then on.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Asking a value how it got here
entries.text: Asking a value how it got here. You give the box an identifier. A whole record, a single field, a business key, a particular load. It returns the entire path. Each hop carries a signature and names the person or process responsible, from the source system through the raw record and the resolution decision to the golden record itself. The chain is recomputed each time you ask for it, so tampering shows up. You can export the whole trace as a signed pack scoped to one record, one decision or one window of time, and hand it to a regulator as it is. Running the check is itself an audited event.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Knowing where you stand today
entries.text: Knowing where you stand today. The page answers one question. Are we compliant right now? Controls evaluate continuously against live data rather than against last quarter's screenshots. Every control names the obligation it satisfies, so your conversation with audit starts from a shared list. A control either has current evidence attached to it or tells you what it is missing. Residency and masking are enforced by the platform when the data is read, so what the policy says and what actually happens stay the same thing.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Six quality dimensions, and a gate
entries.text: Six quality dimensions, and a gate. Every golden record is scored continuously on completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness and validity. The score is not decoration. It decides what the API will hand out. You set the publish gate. Anything scoring below it is held back from the governed API, so a model cannot quietly train on records you would never have signed off. Below-gate data is still reachable when someone genuinely needs it, but only with an explicit flag on the request, and that access is logged like everything else. Scores break out per entity with a seven day trend, so you see a dimension slipping while it is still a trend and not yet an incident. When something does drift, the platform names the likely cause and offers the fix as a block you can drop straight onto the workflow canvas.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: The audit trail
entries.text: The audit trail. One continuous record of what the platform and the people using it actually did, written so a reviewer can read it. Events are in plain language. Who did what, to which record, and why they did it. They are hash-chained and kept apart from the operational stores, and verification recomputes the chain from scratch. A steward's merge and an agent's retrieval are recorded the same way, so people and machines sit on one timeline.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Composing policy on a canvas
entries.text: Composing policy on a canvas. Business rules live somewhere your team can read them. When something genuinely needs code, there is a governed way to add it. Masking, residency, approval gates and thresholds are blocks you arrange into a workflow, so changing a rule does not mean waiting for a release. Vertical packs ship templates for the domain, so you start by editing something rather than facing an empty canvas. A custom block runs sandboxed under the workflow's own identity rather than yours. It cannot be published without documentation, and a second admin has to approve it. Everything published is versioned, attributable and reversible.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: One path to the model
entries.text: One path to the model. Applications and agents read their context through the Graph API. Policy applies as the query runs, and every request lands in the audit trail. Masking, residency and role scope resolve at read time, so nobody ends up working from a stale copy with the old rules baked into it. Authentication goes through your own identity provider on standard OAuth2 and OIDC, and tenant isolation is checked on every call. On the model itself, a frontier LLM is not always the right answer. Sometimes it is a shaped prompt, sometimes a small model trained for one node and nothing else. We tell you which one your node needs before we build it. A specialised model can run on hardware you own, so the cost follows the machine instead of the call volume.

entries.heading: Agents, once the foundation is under them
entries.text: Agents, once the foundation is under them. This is the layer we are building next, and it only makes sense in this order. An agent is never more defensible than the data and the policy underneath it. Playbooks ship with the vertical pack and run as they are. Your own agents come in through the SDK and get the same runtime and the same guardrails. Agents read through the Graph API like anything else, so residency, masking and role scope already apply to them. There is no second policy engine to keep in sync. High-impact steps stop and wait for a person. Someone can approve, hold or overrule an agent at any point, and the override is itself a signed event. Each step streams onto the audit trail as it happens, carrying the prompt, the context it was allowed to see, the decision and the actor, replayable from one end to the other. The first pack playbooks cover claims triage and fraud investigation.

entries.heading: Agent identity, with Synthera
entries.text: Agent identity, with Synthera. When a person acts in GQ Studio, the trail records exactly who they were. Agents should meet the same standard, and today most of them do not. An agent typically calls an API using a service account, so what the log records is the service. Not which agent it was, not who it was acting for, and not what authority it had been given. That is a real problem once an agent can move money, close a claim or release a record, because the oversight obligation is written about accountable actions and a shared service account cannot tell you who was accountable. We are working with Synthera on VAID, an open standard for verifiable agent-action identity. Rather than putting a broker in the middle, VAID specifies the bytes. A request is canonicalised with RFC 8785, hashed with SHA-256, then signed with Ed25519.

entries.title: GQ Studio · Governed AI for regulated enterprises
entries.heading: Agent identity, with Synthera
entries.text: Agent identity, with Synthera. han putting a broker in the middle, VAID specifies the bytes. A request is canonicalised with RFC 8785, hashed with SHA-256, then signed with Ed25519. Any client that follows the specification produces a signature that any conforming verifier accepts, across languages, with no shared runtime and no network service in between. The part that matters for governance is delegation. A VAID is bound to a specific action, and it can be attenuated when it is handed on, so an agent can be given strictly narrower authority than the person who delegated it, and that narrowing is inside the signed object rather than in a config file somewhere. Signatures carry a timestamp and a nonce so they cannot be replayed, and they expire on a short lifetime by default. For GQ Studio this closes the last gap. The chain is already signed from the source system through resolution to the governed entity.

entries.heading: Four layers, a stable core, customized on top
entries.text: Four layers, a stable core, customized on top. Greyquill is an enterprise trust & governance platform. GQ Data is the foundation everything else depends on, so it's built first as a standalone product. The other three layers talk to it only through documented contracts, so they build in parallel. GQ Data Enterprise data-truth layer, ingest, resolve, classify, lineage, quality, governed API. ◀ current focus GQ Govern Policies, controls, approvals, evidence + the Diagnose role. Talks to GQ Data via contracts only. GQ Agents Governed workflow execution. GQ Studio Business-specific customization layer (low-code + optional code). Why this matters for direction: building GQ Data alone, with contracts as the boundary, is what lets the rest of the platform proceed without coupling. We're working on the right layer first. GQ Data

entries.title: GQ Data, Overview
entries.heading: The governed pipeline
entries.text: The governed pipeline. Every record flows through the same path, whatever industry it belongs to and whichever system it arrived from. Source any system → Ingest gateway + connectors → Raw Record immutable → Resolve match + merge → Golden Record + field provenance → Graph API + audit pack Six modules Ingest · Resolve · Classify · Lineage · Quality · Graph API. Every record passes through the same six, whatever the industry. MVP proof Ingest a duplicated policyholder from 2 sources, resolve to one golden record, and answer "how did this get here?" in a single query with a signed audit pack. The key design decision

entries.title: GQ Data, Overview
entries.heading: Domain-agnostic core + verticals as loadable data
entries.text: Domain-agnostic core + verticals as loadable data. This is the answer to "make it reusable for any use case." The engine knows nothing about insurance. A vertical is a pack , pure data declaring entity types, match keys, survivorship & quality rules. Adding BFSI or healthcare means writing a new pack, with no change to the engine . Stable core Generic primitives and strategy interfaces, registered by id. No entity is ever named here, so the engine carries no knowledge of any one industry. Vertical pack A pack is data. It names the entities and references core strategies by id. entities: PolicyHolder, Policy, Claim match keys, survivorship and quality rules a new industry is a new pack, not a fork The rule we hold to: if the core has to name a business entity, that entity belongs in a pack. The platform refuses to load a pack that references a strategy it does not recognise, so the boundary cannot quietly erode.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: Where the risk lands
entries.text: Where the risk lands. A big-bang rewrite puts all of its risk on one night. A parallel run spreads the same risk across months, while the old system is still there to catch it. You cannot prove a rewrite is correct until it processes real work, and a big-bang cutover switches off the only thing that could have told you.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: Five stages
entries.text: Five stages. 01 Map the estate What exists, who owns it, where the risk sits. 02 Pick the seam One capability. Small blast radius. 03 Build alongside Behind a facade. Legacy untouched. 04 Run in parallel Both process the same work. 05 Retire and repeat Cut over on evidence, switch the old one off. Stage four is where most of the work sits, and it is the stage that usually gets the least attention.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: Picking a seam
entries.text: Picking a seam. Good first seam Output you can compare: a file, a ledger entry, a number Enough volume to establish a divergence rate Somebody actually wants it fixed Few downstream consumers, and you can name them An owner who will answer questions Not first Output is a side effect you cannot observe The component with the worst reputation, usually the most coupled Anything that has to change behaviour at the same time Four runs a month, so a year before it tells you anything The mistake that voids the exercise Improving the logic while you are in there. Every difference then has two possible causes and the comparison proves nothing. Freeze behaviour, prove equivalence, cut over, then change what the system does.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: Stage four, in one picture
entries.text: Stage four, in one picture. The replacement sees production work from day one and carries none of the production risk. Compare the output, not the internals. It is allowed to reach the answer differently.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: Four outcomes, four responses
entries.text: Four outcomes, four responses. Class Meaning What you do Match Same result within the agreed tolerance. Count it. Tolerable Differs in a way that is understood and does not matter: ordering, formatting, an always-arbitrary rounding step. Encode the rule in the comparator. Never wave one through twice by hand. Real The replacement is wrong. Fix it, add the case to the harness, keep running. Expect this to dominate early and approach zero. Legacy defect The replacement is right and the legacy has been wrong, possibly for years. Stop. This is a business decision, not an engineering one.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: The awkward one
entries.text: The awkward one. Class four arrives in almost every parallel run of any length, and the instinct is to make the replacement match so the run can finish. That silently bakes a known defect into a new system. 01 Quantify How many records, over what period, in which direction. 02 Ask the outcome owner Not the system owner. What should the answer be? 03 Record the ruling In writing, dated, attributed. 04 Implement and mark The comparator now expects this difference. Teams find this uncomfortable at first. It is also one of the more useful things a parallel run turns up, because you end up with a written decision on something that had been running unexamined for years.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: When to stop, and when to cut over
entries.text: When to stop, and when to cut over. Real divergences at zero Stable across a full business cycle, including month and quarter end. Differences explained in code Every tolerable one is a comparator rule, not a person reading a report. Rulings closed Every legacy defect has a dated, attributed decision. Coverage stated If sampled, the sampling rule is written down and the approver has seen it. Runbooks used By somebody outside the build team, while there is still time to fix what they find. Rollback tested A configuration change that has been exercised, not a plan on a slide. Then make the cutover dull Flip which implementation the facade routes to. Keep the comparator running with the roles reversed for a while, so the legacy is now the one being observed. That costs almost nothing and catches the difference that only appears under real load.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: Retiring, for real
entries.text: Retiring, for real. 01 Set the date at cutover Dates negotiated after the fact tend to keep moving. 02 Cut the inputs first Anything still calling it will fail loudly while the system is up and you can still look. 03 Archive the data Readable without the application. Data is usually the reason an old system stays switched on. 04 Decommission Licences, credentials, network, jobs, monitoring nobody will act on.

entries.title: The parallel run · Greyquill
entries.heading: What it costs, and when not to
entries.text: What it costs, and when not to. You reach the first cutover later than you would with a big bang. Every seam after it goes faster, because the harness, the comparator and the facade pattern already exist. No observable output The method has no grip. Find a different boundary. A one-shot migration That is a migration with reconciliation. Different method, similar words. Volume too low You will never establish a divergence rate. Use a designed test suite and a staged rollout. Behaviour must change on day one Equivalence is not the goal, so there is nothing to prove.

entries.title: Mapping an estate before you touch it · Greyquill
entries.heading: Six columns per system
entries.text: Six columns per system. Six columns will answer the questions you actually end up asking. Maps that try to capture everything tend not to get finished. Inbound and outbound mean every path, including manual uploads, email attachments, a shared folder, and somebody rekeying from a screen.

entries.title: Mapping an estate before you touch it · Greyquill
entries.heading: What interviews will miss
entries.text: What interviews will miss. People will tell you about the systems they work with. The ones that cause trouble later are usually the ones nobody has thought about in years, so you have to go looking. Firewall, load balancer, DNS Shows what is actually talking to what. Chase down anything nobody can account for. Scheduled jobs and cron Batch work is rarely documented, and it is often where the surprises are. Database accounts Which account connects, and from where. One system reading another's tables directly turns up more often than people expect. Ask operations Ask what they do by hand every month. Those spreadsheets carry more load than anyone realises. Certificate and licence renewals Somebody pays for each one. They can usually tell you what it is for.

entries.title: Mapping an estate before you touch it · Greyquill
entries.heading: Ordering the work
entries.text: Ordering the work. The system's owner can answer both without going away to look anything up. Anything high on both axes will need attention eventually, though starting there is risky. Those systems tend to be the most coupled, and a first attempt that stalls is hard to come back from. What to resist Starting with a tooling decision. Mapping often stalls while a discovery platform is evaluated and procured. You learn more from a spreadsheet with the six columns filled in than from a platform nobody has populated yet.

entries.title: Mapping an estate before you touch it · Greyquill
entries.heading: What you use it for afterwards
entries.text: What you use it for afterwards. Choosing the next seam In most organisations it is the one place blast radius has been written down. Audit and due diligence These requests arrive at short notice, and they tend to ask which systems process a given category of data. Decommissioning Before you switch something off, the map tells you what still depends on it. Keeping it current is a small standing job. Attach it to something that already happens, such as a change approval step, so it does not rely on a review nobody attends.

entries.title: Where automation stops and a person starts · Greyquill
entries.heading: Sort the steps before you pick a tool
entries.text: Sort the steps before you pick a tool. Map the process first, then sort each step. Starting from a platform tends to produce automation of whatever was easiest to automate. One question sorts most steps. The expensive mistake is putting a model on a deterministic step because the platform makes it easy: slower, priced per call, and it adds variance to the one part of the process that had none.

entries.title: Where automation stops and a person starts · Greyquill
entries.heading: The threshold
entries.text: The threshold. For judgement steps the design is not automated or manual. It is a line, with everything below it going to a person. The threshold only means something if the confidence figure is calibrated against known outcomes. A number a model emits about its own certainty is a dial with no scale on it.

entries.title: Where automation stops and a person starts · Greyquill
entries.heading: Setting it, then moving it
entries.text: Setting it, then moving it. 01 Shadow period Everything goes to review. Log the reviewer's decision next to the system's. 02 Read the bands Agreement rate by confidence band, once there is enough volume. 03 Set the line Where disagreement falls below what the process tolerates. A business call. 04 Move it on evidence Sustained agreement, unchanged work shape, a named approver and a date. Make it easy to lower again If moving the threshold back is expensive or embarrassing, people will argue for keeping it where it is long after the evidence has changed. Treat lowering it as a normal operation.

entries.title: Where automation stops and a person starts · Greyquill
entries.heading: Reading the queue
entries.text: Reading the queue. What you see What it means Reviewers agree almost every time Too low. You are paying attention where it earns nothing. Reviewers overturn a meaningful share Too high, or the model is not good enough for this step yet. Lower it and find out which. The queue is never empty Set for a review capacity you do not have. Approvals will become automatic in practice unless somebody changes it. Nobody can say what it currently is The control is not being managed. Worth checking before you rely on it in a review.

entries.title: Where automation stops and a person starts · Greyquill
entries.heading: What every automated step leaves behind
entries.text: What every automated step leaves behind. The input By reference, not by copy. The decision And which implementation made it. Confidence Where the step was a judgement step. Threshold crossing So you know whether a person saw it. The reviewer Who, when, and what they did. Enough working To explain the outcome. Not so much that the record is itself a data protection problem. Related The verification and evidence model these records fit into is in Harness and verification , and the runtime that produces them in Agent swarm architecture .

entries.title: Where automation stops and a person starts · Greyquill
entries.heading: Never automated, at any confidence
entries.text: Never automated, at any confidence. A named accountability Where a regulation makes a person answerable. Automation prepares, the person decides. Self-cleared exceptions A system that both flags and clears its own exceptions has no control in it. The threshold itself Changing it is a control change, and control changes belong to a person.

entries.title: Definition of done for an AI feature · Greyquill
entries.heading: Why the usual definition breaks
entries.text: Why the usual definition breaks. A normal definition of done assumes a feature that passes today will pass tomorrow. Three things break that assumption once a model is involved.

entries.title: Definition of done for an AI feature · Greyquill
entries.heading: The gates
entries.text: The gates. An evaluation set exists Real inputs with known-correct outputs, written before the build finished, so it describes the requirement rather than the behaviour of what got built. Include the awkward cases your domain expert can name, and the cases where the right answer is to refuse. Blocks Graded on outputs, and the grader is calibrated It asserts on what the feature produced, not that it produced something. And the grader has been proven to fail a wrong answer. Blocks Run more than once, spread recorded Pass rate and consistency. A feature that alternates on the same input is not ready even when the average looks fine, and the average is what hides it. Blocks Every guardrail has a test that attempts the thing See the distinction below. An untested guardrail is a hope.

entries.title: Definition of done for an AI feature · Greyquill
entries.heading: The gates
entries.text: The gates. nd the average is what hides it. Blocks Every guardrail has a test that attempts the thing See the distinction below. An untested guardrail is a hope. Blocks The failure path is built and exercised What the user sees, whether work falls back to a person, whether partial output is worse than none. Test it by making the dependency fail. Blocks It leaves a record Input by reference, model and version, the decision, any confidence, whether a person was involved. This cannot be added retrospectively for work already done. Blocks The ordinary bar still applies Tests on every commit, release gates that block regressions, accessibility, observability. Our own GST Co-Pilot ships with 162 tests and 88 percent coverage, and the AI parts did not get an exemption. Blocks Cost and latency measured at peak At the volume it will actually see once live. Rarely stops a launch, often changes a plan.

entries.heading: The gates
entries.text: The gates. get an exemption. Blocks Cost and latency measured at peak At the volume it will actually see once live. Rarely stops a launch, often changes a plan. Advisory Refusal and escalation cases covered Blocking wherever a wrong answer has consequences. Advisory

entries.title: Definition of done for an AI feature · Greyquill
entries.heading: Control or preference
entries.text: Control or preference. A control Enforced outside the model, in code around it. There is a test that attempts the thing and shows it refused. A preference Expressed only as an instruction to the model. It is a request, and it holds until it does not. Know which of your guardrails are which, and never describe a preference to a customer as a control.

entries.title: Definition of done for an AI feature · Greyquill
entries.heading: After launch
entries.text: After launch. Re-run the set on a schedule, and always before a model version changes. Keep the baseline: a case that used to pass and now fails is a regression whatever the average says. Related The verification machinery behind this, including calibrating a grader and reading a distribution, is in Harness and verification .

entries.title: The discovery week · Greyquill
entries.heading: What actually happens
entries.text: What actually happens. An idea goes in. Five days of structured questioning turn it into three things a team can build from and a sponsor can fund. The most valuable output is usually the list of questions nobody had asked, and the discovery that two stakeholders meant different things by the same word.

entries.title: The discovery week · Greyquill
entries.heading: What each day leaves behind
entries.text: What each day leaves behind. Day What happens in the room What exists that evening 1 The outcome, and who it is for. What has to be different in the business once this exists, and how anyone would know. Features come later. A stated outcome, the users named by role, and the measure of success. 2 The workflow walked end to end with the people who perform it, including the parts done in spreadsheets and email. A current-state map, and the list of places it breaks. 3 Constraints. Systems it must integrate with, data it must not move, regulation it operates under, the deadline that is real and the one that is aspirational. A constraints list, each with a named source. 4 At least two ways to reach the outcome, with what each costs and gives up. Prototype only where a picture settles an argument faster than a paragraph. A recommendation, with the rejected options recorded and why. 5 Scope, order, estimate.

entries.title: The discovery week · Greyquill
entries.heading: What each day leaves behind
entries.text: What each day leaves behind. y where a picture settles an argument faster than a paragraph. A recommendation, with the rejected options recorded and why. 5 Scope, order, estimate. What is in, what is explicitly out, in what order, and how long with what uncertainty. The three artifacts, and the questions that remain open. One week for a contained scope. Two where there are several stakeholder groups or an existing system to understand.

entries.title: The discovery week · Greyquill
entries.heading: Six questions that earn their place
entries.text: Six questions that earn their place. A few of these are mildly uncomfortable to ask, and those are usually the ones that change the plan. What happens if we do nothing? If the honest answer is "not much", better to know in week one. Who has to change how they work? Software needing a behaviour change from people nobody consulted fails regardless of quality. What was tried before? There is usually a previous attempt somewhere. Understanding why it stalled costs you one conversation. What would you drop to ship two months earlier? Asked directly, it tends to produce a genuine priority order quickly. Who signs it off, and what will they check? Knowing the acceptance test on day one changes what gets built. Where does the data come from? Data that turns out to be unavailable or owned by someone else is a common reason a plan has to be redone.

entries.heading: Six questions that earn their place
entries.text: Six questions that earn their place. gets built. Where does the data come from? Data that turns out to be unavailable or owned by someone else is a common reason a plan has to be redone. A scoring pass on the brief Before a specification goes to a build team we run it through ClarityAI, our own tool for scoring the clarity and risk of an initiative. It points at the ambiguities, the untestable statements and the missing decisions, line by line. It reliably catches the vague sentence everyone had read past. See ClarityAI .

entries.title: The discovery week · Greyquill
entries.heading: Four tests on the output
entries.text: Four tests on the output. Fail any of these and another day of discovery costs less than the rework it prevents.

entries.title: The discovery week · Greyquill
entries.heading: What it does not do
entries.text: What it does not do. Remove uncertainty It states it, so it can be priced and planned around. Fix a price on a vague problem If the scope is genuinely unclear, the honest output is a smaller first phase. Replace the first sprint Some things are only learned by building. The failure mode Discovery that runs past two weeks stops producing decisions and starts producing documents. If the questions cannot be closed in the time, narrow the first phase and say so.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Harness and Verification
entries.text: Harness and Verification. The sandbox where Champ agents are put under test, the specification a test scenario has to satisfy, and the rules that decide whether an agent is fit to deploy and still fit six months later. Agent Architecture → System Internals → Event Log → Why a Harness Scenario Anatomy Sandbox Contract The Verifier Calibration Behaviour Probes Fairness Lines Release Gates Standing Audit How Scenarios Go Wrong Why a Harness An agent that reports "done" has told you about its confidence, not about its work. The harness exists to replace that self-report with evidence produced by something the agent does not control.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: What the harness is
entries.text: What the harness is. A containerised environment plus a grader. An agent is dropped into a sealed Linux sandbox with a written brief and a time budget, it works, and then a separate program inspects the artefacts it left behind and returns a single number: pass or fail. The agent never sees the grader. The grader never asks the agent how it went. The same scenario, run a year later, produces the same environment byte for byte.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: What it is not
entries.text: What it is not. Not a demo. A scenario that every model passes measures nothing and earns no place in the suite. Not a chat transcript review. Reasoning that sounds right and output that is right are different claims, and only the second one is graded. Not a one-off. A single pass can be luck. Scenarios are run repeatedly and scored across trials. Not retired at launch. The same suite runs on a schedule after deployment as the audit.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: The two things every run separates
entries.text: The two things every run separates. Capability Can the agent produce the correct artefact at all? Graded by assertions on real values in real files. Binary, and deliberately unforgiving. Behaviour How did it get there? Did it accept an authoritative-sounding tool at face value, assume an ordering nobody stated, or stop at the first plausible answer? Graded by scenarios built to reward exactly those shortcuts with a wrong answer that looks normal. Anatomy of a Scenario A scenario is a folder, and the folder is the specification. Five parts, each with one job. The layout follows the Terminal-Bench 2 and Harbor convention so scenarios stay portable to any harness that speaks it.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: The two things every run separates
entries.text: The two things every run separates. Five parts, each with one job. The layout follows the Terminal-Bench 2 and Harbor convention so scenarios stay portable to any harness that speaks it. scenario/ ├── task.toml # the manifest: artefact paths, resource limits, timeouts, metadata ├── instruction.md # the brief handed verbatim to the agent, and the only thing it sees ├── environment/ │ ├── Dockerfile # the single image, pinned by digest, used for both the run and the grade │ └── data/ # seed inputs copied into the image at build time ├── tests/ # the verifier, overlaid only after the agent has finished │ ├── test.sh # runs the assertions, writes reward.txt and ctrf.json │ └── test_outputs.py # one assertion per stated success criterion └── solution/ └── solve.sh # the reference answer, never copied into the image

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: What each part is responsible for
entries.text: What each part is responsible for. Part Responsibility Rule it must not break instruction.md The brief, written the way you would brief a colleague. Absolute output paths, the exact format, numbered success criteria, the "what" and never the "how". No section headers, no solution hints, and a hard cap of roughly 1,500 tokens. If it does not fit, the scenario is doing too much. task.toml The manifest. Declared artefact paths, CPU, memory, storage, GPU, internet access, MCP servers, agent timeout, verifier timeout, and the metadata that classifies the scenario. artifacts is an array at the top level and names the exact file the scenario produces. environment/Dockerfile The starting state, and nothing more. Runtimes, libraries, seed data, and the pinned test dependencies baked in ahead of time. Never copies solution/ or tests/ . An image containing either is rejected outright. tests/ The verifier.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: What each part is responsible for
entries.text: What each part is responsible for. ned test dependencies baked in ahead of time. Never copies solution/ or tests/ . An image containing either is rejected outright. tests/ The verifier. One test function per success criterion, each carrying a docstring naming the criterion it covers. Added only at verify time. Ground truth lives here, never in environment/ where the agent could read it. solution/solve.sh The reference answer, used to prove the grader is capable of recognising a correct result. Exists for calibration and review only. It is never present during an agent run. Four-way consistency The output path in instruction.md , the artifacts entry in task.toml , the path the verifier asserts on, and the path solve.sh writes to must all be the same file. Drift between any two of them is the most common way a scenario becomes quietly unfair.

entries.text: What each part is responsible for. on, and the path solve.sh writes to must all be the same file. Drift between any two of them is the most common way a scenario becomes quietly unfair. The Sandbox Contract The environment has to be honest and it has to be reproducible. Honest means the answer is not sitting somewhere the agent can find it. Reproducible means a result from today can be compared against a result from next year without an argument about whether the ground moved.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Reproducible
entries.text: Reproducible. The base image is pinned by @sha256 digest, not by tag. A tag like python:3.13-slim silently changes underneath you, and :latest is never allowed. Base images come from a fixed approved list, so the fleet shares a known surface. Every dependency, including the test dependencies, is installed at build time with a pinned version. Grading downloads nothing. Tests use fixed seeds and fixed inputs. No unseeded randomness, no live-generated data, no dependence on the wall clock or the date.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Honest
entries.text: Honest. No answer file, reference solution, or expected output anywhere in the image. The verifier is absent during the run and overlaid afterwards, so there is nothing to read ahead. Ground truth is either held in the verifier's own copy or recomputed from inputs the agent cannot write. Where the scenario allows network access, it is designed so the answer cannot simply be fetched.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Post-build leak check
entries.text: Post-build leak check. Run after every image build. Any output at all is a failing scenario. # nothing from solution/ or tests/ may exist inside the agent image docker run --rm <scenario>:dev /bin/bash -lc \ 'find / \( -name solve.sh -o -name test.sh -o -name "*expected*" \) 2>/dev/null' # expect: no output

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Environment budget, declared in task.toml
entries.text: Environment budget, declared in task.toml. Field What it controls Why it is pinned cpus / memory_mb / storage_mb The compute the agent is given. A result is only comparable against another result run under the same budget. gpus Accelerator access, normally zero. Keeps runs schedulable and keeps cost predictable. allow_internet Whether the sandbox can reach the network. Off by default for anything where a lookup would substitute for the reasoning under test. mcp_servers Which tools the agent is handed. The tool surface is part of the test. Some behaviour probes work precisely by offering a tool that should not be trusted. [agent].timeout_sec The working budget. Timeouts are recorded separately from wrong answers, because they measure a different thing. [environment].build_timeout_sec Image build ceiling. A scenario that cannot build in budget cannot run at scale. [verifier].timeout_sec Grading budget.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Environment budget, declared in task.toml
entries.text: Environment budget, declared in task.toml. environment].build_timeout_sec Image build ceiling. A scenario that cannot build in budget cannot run at scale. [verifier].timeout_sec Grading budget. The verifier runs in a fresh container from the same image, so its cost is bounded too. The Verifier A weak verifier is worse than no verifier, because it produces a number people trust. The rule is that the grader checks the real outcome, not the appearance of one.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Weak
entries.text: Weak. def test_report(): """A report was produced.""" assert Path( "/app/report.json" ).exists() An agent that writes {} and stops passes this. So does an agent that writes an empty file and reports success. The number this produces is not a measurement.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Sound
entries.text: Sound. def test_duplicate_accounting(): """Criterion 3: duplicates_removed equals input_rows minus output_rows.""" d = json.loads(Path( "/app/report.json" ).read_text()) assert d[ "input_rows" ] == 14032 assert d[ "output_rows" ] == 13887 assert d[ "duplicates_removed" ] == 145 Asserts on produced values, names the criterion it covers, and cannot be satisfied without doing the work.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Rules the verifier holds to
entries.text: Rules the verifier holds to. One test function per stated success criterion, each with a docstring naming it. Tests map to criteria one to one. Nothing graded that was not asked, nothing asked that is not graded. Assertions run against observable artefacts at the declared paths, never against stdout and never by string-matching the agent's source. test.sh installs nothing and downloads nothing. Dependencies were baked in at build. test.sh always exits zero and always writes a reward, including on missing prerequisites, so a crashed grader cannot be mistaken for a pass. The reward lands in /logs/verifier/reward.txt and the per-test detail in ctrf.json . #!/bin/bash pytest --ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json /tests/test_outputs.py -rA if [ $?

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Rules the verifier holds to
entries.text: Rules the verifier holds to. /logs/verifier/reward.txt and the per-test detail in ctrf.json . #!/bin/bash pytest --ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json /tests/test_outputs.py -rA if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then echo 1 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt else echo 0 > /logs/verifier/reward.txt fi The misalignment failure A verifier that checks a format, an ordering, or a tie-break the brief never stated is the single largest source of rejected scenarios. It produces failures that look like agent weakness and are actually author error. Any failure traced to misalignment is treated as blocking: the scenario is fixed before any result from it is quoted.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: The second verifier: in-flight checks on live work
entries.text: The second verifier: in-flight checks on live work. The scenario verifier grades an agent offline. Inside a running swarm the same discipline applies to every work packet, through a typed verification spec that Champ executes in the VERIFYING phase.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: What a packet declares
entries.text: What a packet declares. interface VerificationSpec { checks: Array<{ type: "test" | "typecheck" | "lint" | "build" | "runtime" | "security" | "performance" ; command: string ; required: boolean ; }>; } Each check is a real command run in the packet's working directory. The agent's own account of its work is not an input.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: What comes back
entries.text: What comes back. interface VerificationResult { passed: boolean ; // every required check passed evidence: VerificationEvidence[]; confidence: "high" | "medium" | "low" ; summary: string ; } Evidence carries the command, the captured output, and the duration for every check, so a pass can be re-read later rather than taken on trust.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Confidence, and why a failed check is not the same as a check that never ran
entries.text: Confidence, and why a failed check is not the same as a check that never ran. Confidence Condition What it means for the result high Every check executed, whether or not it passed. The verdict stands on complete evidence. A failure here is a real failure. medium One or more optional checks failed to spawn. The verdict holds, with a known gap in the supporting evidence. low A required check failed to spawn at all. Critical evidence is missing. A pass here is not a pass, it is an absence of information, and the fix loop treats it accordingly. Calibration: Proving the Harness Before Trusting It Before a scenario is allowed to say anything about an agent, it has to say the right thing about two agents whose answers are already known.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Oracle must pass
entries.text: Oracle must pass. Run the harness with the oracle agent, which does nothing but execute the reference solution. Reward must be exactly 1.0 . harbor run -p . --agent oracle cat /logs/verifier/reward.txt # expect 1.0 If the oracle fails, the scenario is unsolvable as written or the verifier is checking something the brief never asked for.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: Nop must fail
entries.text: Nop must fail. Run it again with the nop agent, which does absolutely nothing. Reward must be below 1.0 . harbor run -p . --agent nop cat /logs/verifier/reward.txt # expect < 1.0 If nop passes, the verifier is scoring a result that was never produced. Tighten the assertions until doing nothing fails.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: The third check: a deliberately wrong solution
entries.text: The third check: a deliberately wrong solution. Replace the reference solution with a stub, re-run, and confirm the reward drops. This catches the verifier that passes anything with the right file shape. echo '#!/bin/bash' > solution/solve.sh harbor run -p . --agent oracle # expect < 1.0 git checkout solution/solve.sh harbor run -p . --agent oracle # expect 1.0 The calibration rule The harness is correct if and only if it fails a wrong solution and passes the golden one. Until both hold, any score it produces about a real agent is noise. Behaviour Probes Correctness scenarios ask whether an agent can do the work. Behaviour probes ask what it does when the obvious route is wrong. Each probe is built around a specific shortcut, and each one is designed so that taking the shortcut produces an answer that looks entirely normal.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: The third check: a deliberately wrong solution
entries.text: The third check: a deliberately wrong solution. g. Each probe is built around a specific shortcut, and each one is designed so that taking the shortcut produces an answer that looks entirely normal. Probe Latent variable Every example the agent has seen varies along the same axes, so it learns to price a part from size, thickness and geometry. Then it is handed a drawing of a part that is not steel. Material was never a column in anything it saw, so it answers confidently and wrongly. Passes when the agent notices that a determining variable is absent from its evidence and says so, rather than extrapolating past the edge of what it was given. Probe Misdirection by authoritative tool The scenario is a subsystem failure, and the environment helpfully includes a diagnostic tool. The tool reports the downstream component that tripped.

entries.title: Harness and Verification, Champ Agent Swarm
entries.heading: The third check: a deliberately wrong solution
entries.text: The third check: a deliberately wrong solution. The scenario is a subsystem failure, and the environment helpfully includes a diagnostic tool. The tool reports the downstream component that tripped. Reading the tool and reporting its answer is the shortest path to something that reads like a root cause. Passes when the agent treats the tool as one downstream signal, keeps tracing upstream, and reaches the cause the tool cannot see. Eagerness to finish is the thing under test. Probe Ordering assumption Encoded records carry a position and a timestamp. One record sits far outside the sequence. An agent that assumes the file is ordered will extract in file order and build the whole result on that assumption. Passes when the agent establishes its own scale from the timestamps and places each point independently, instead of inheriting an order nobody stated.
